subject: penguin
pitch: An emperor penguin chick's proud parent. Glossy blue-black back and head, a crisp white belly blending into a warm golden-yellow patch at the neck and ear, a long slender beak with an orange-pink stripe, stubby flippers held slightly out, and big black feet. A fluffy grey chick peeks out from between its feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning the scene with a TypeScript module using the agentic-3js-builder SDK, thinking through realistic proportions—adult emperor penguins around 1.1-1.2m tall with chicks much smaller at hatching, roughly 0.3m.

I'm working out placement with chick standing on the ground between the adult's feet, peeking forward, and setting up coordinates with +Y up and the penguin facing +Z. I'm detailing the plumage accurately: glossy black-blue dorsal coloring, white belly, the distinctive golden-orange ear patches and neck markings, black bill with its characteristic orange-pink stripe, and dark flippers with white undersides.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy, placing the root hips joint low near the floor since penguin legs are mostly hidden inside the body, then building a spine chain upward through the torso to a short neck and head to capture that upright, egg-shaped posture. I'm planning to construct the body as a lofted tube shape following a smooth curved path to get that characteristic oval penguin silhouette.

I'm thinking hips should be the root joint with role "spine," positioned at the pelvis, and then a chain running up through chest and neck to form the torso, with each catmull span becoming its own joint along that path.

I'll keep the body mostly upright with a slight forward lean, defining path points from hips through chest and neck up to the head. Using four points gives three spans plus a tip joint, so I'll name them "hips," "chest," "neck," and "head," where the head tip naturally aims along the path's ending tangent.

I'm thinking the body should be lofted and skinned across the full chain, while the head gets built separately—maybe an egg-shaped lathe or loft with its own stations—then attached at the tip joint so it sits naturally atop the neck.

For the coloring, I want a stylized penguin look: dark blue-black back, white belly, split based on the surface normal's forward-facing component with a smooth transition, plus a small golden patch near the neck/ear area where the normal faces sideways and the height matches the head region.

I confirm `paint` is the constructor imported from the single SDK module along with everything else like `noise`, `smoothstep`, and `mix`, since all exports come from one package. I also note the typecheck rejects unused parameters, so I'll prefix unused ones with underscores, and I start planning the penguin's coloring, like a glossy blue-black for the back and head.

Now I'm picking specific hex colors for each part: a bluish-black back and head, a white belly, a golden-yellow ear patch, and a black bill with an orange-pink stripe. I'm figuring out how to paint that stripe along the side of the beak using angular coordinates on the sweep geometry.

For the stubby flippers, I'm planning to use a joint chain (shoulder, elbow, wrist, tip) swept along with a flattened cross-section to give them a flipper-like shape held slightly outward.

I work out the right axis convention: drawing the outline in the plane spanned by forward and up gives a side-view paddle shape thin along the lateral axis, then tilting the up axis slightly outward (scaled by the mirror sign) splays the flipper's length away from the body for a natural resting pose.

Now I need to anchor the flipper root onto the body surface itself -- the chest is roughly 0.36 wide, so the flipper should attach around x ±0.18 and extend down toward the hips near y ~0.45, with the splay carrying the tip further outward as it descends.

For the feet, I'm thinking of modeling them as flat horizontal extrusions since emperor penguins have short legs mostly hidden in the body, with webbed, forward-pointing toes sticking out at the base. I'll set the outline plane to run right (x) and forward (y), which puts the extrusion thickness vertically (along y) -- giving a flattened webbed-triangle foot shape with spreading toes.

For the leg itself, I'm sketching a chain from hip to knee to ankle using a catmull path with three named joints, since a foot should be the tip of its leg chain. I'm placing approximate coordinates for hip, knee, and ankle on each side to keep the legs mostly tucked under the body as they are in real emperor penguins.

I'm also reconsidering the body loft's vertical extent so it properly extends down toward where the feet meet the floor, planning to define explicit stations along the spine path rather than letting the hips chain handle that alone.

For the loft geometry, I'm reasoning that since the spine path runs vertically, the cross-section plane must be horizontal, so width (w) maps to the X-axis and height (h) maps to Z-depth rather than vertical extent — meaning the loft's bottom cap shape depends on how the stations and end caps are handled, not on the "h" parameter controlling vertical reach.

I'm now considering using sweep instead of loft, since sweep accepts a radius function returning [rx, ry] per station along the path, letting me taper the body profile — small radius near the bottom and top, widening at the belly — to get a natural egg-like penguin silhouette with rounded caps.

For dimensions, I'm thinking emperor penguins are plump but slender from the front: roughly 0.18-0.2 half-width at the chest, slightly less in depth, narrowing toward the head and tapering at the neck, with a round head sitting on top and a beak projecting forward-down.

I'm now working out the local coordinate frame convention for an upward-pointing bone so the head's forward-facing beak and jaw joint get the right orientation relative to the body.

I'm sizing the head as a sphere with moderate segments for a stylized faceted look, positioning it atop the narrowing neck so it overlaps slightly with the body, and scaling it into a subtle ellipsoid to match realistic emperor penguin proportions.
